paper_context.research_question: Can sentiment features extracted from 10-K Risk Factors (using word-embedding-augmented IR term-weighting schemes) improve company volatility prediction, and how does combining those textual features with market (price-based) features and sector-specific modelling affect predictive performance?
main_claims: Word-embedding-augmented IR term-weighting schemes (e.g., extended BM25, TC variants) applied to finance lexicons substantially improve volatility prediction from 10-K Risk Factors compared to prior lexicon/SVM baselines.

Combining textual sentiment features with market-derived features (current volatility, GARCH) via stacking yields further improvements and more stable long-term volatility forecasts than either modality alone.
Concept drift is present in 10-K reports across years; using more recent subsets (2012–2015) produces better predictive performance than pooling older years.

Sectoral reports display distinct risk-related language; however, training sector-specific models on the current dataset sizes does not beat a general model trained on all sectors (likely due to limited per-sector data).
The proposed method explains a materially larger fraction of variance (higher r2) in first-year volatility than competing state-of-the-art approaches reproduced in the paper.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Predictive performance on volatility (r2, MSE) across time horizons (first year quartiles and later quartiles)
Ablation/comparison of term-weighting schemes (standard vs. embedding-augmented variants) and lexical expansions (Lex vs. LexExt)
Effectiveness of fusion strategies (early fusion, stacking, MKL) for combining text and market features
Robustness to temporal drift (training on older years vs. recent years) and real-world train/test splits
Per-sector performance differences and impact of training set size (sector-specific vs. general vs. sector-agnostic samples)
Computational considerations (e.g., MKL complexity vs. stacking) and dimensionality reduction choices (PCA dimension selection)

Temporal stability and concept drift justification for restricting to 2012–2015 and implications on reported results (Section 6.1).

Test robustness of stacking results: different splits, meta-learner choices, and compare to MKL with full hyperparameter tuning.

Check for temporal leakage: confirm Word2Vec and other models are trained only on appropriate training folds when performing temporal (2013/2014/2015) experiments.
Evaluate the impact of outlier filtering (mean ±3σ) on evaluation metrics and tail-event predictive performance.
Re-run sector-specific vs. sector-agnostic experiments controlling for company-level duplication and sample-size effects (statistical testing).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript argues that embedding-augmented IR term-weighting (notably B̂M25) applied to Loughran-McDonald lexicons yields materially better first-year volatility prediction from 10-K Risk Factors than prior lexicon/SVM baselines; that stacking late-fusion of these textual features with market features further improves r2 and produces more stable long-term forecasts; that concept drift in 10-Ks motivates restricting the main experiments to a recent 2012–2015 subset; and that sector-specific models do not beat a pooled general model given current per-sector sample sizes. The experimental chain depends on a pipeline: (i) heuristic Risk Factors extraction and preprocessing; (ii) Word2Vec trained on all reports for lexicon expansion and embedding-augmentation (Eq.3) with similarity threshold 0.70; (iii) lexicon-weighting schemes (TC, TF, TFIDF, BM25 and their embedding-augmented variants), PCA to 400 dims, SVM-RBF (C=1, ε=0.1) regression; (iv) fusion by stacking, MKL, early fusion; (v) evaluation via 5-fold CV on a 2012–2015 subset (3892 reports). Strengths are empirical gains and multi-angle analysis (fusion, drift, sectors). Key weaknesses / breaks in reasoning include potential temporal leakage (Word2Vec trained on all data), insufficient reporting of extraction accuracy and hyperparameter sensitivity, lack of statistical significance testing, and reliance on ad-hoc choices (70/30 stacking split, PCA=400, similarity threshold 0.70) without ablation. Several claims plausibly hold under the reported experimental setup but are conditionally valid: if preprocessing and embedding training avoid leakage and if stacking/MKL/hyperparameters are robust. The manuscript's novelty appears incremental (adapting embedding-augmented IR weighting from IR literature to financial sentiment prediction) but the domain-specific empirical evaluation and fusion analysis add applied value. I flag where reasoning is strong (internal consistency, multiple baselines) and where it breaks (possible leakage, insufficient sensitivity analyses).
logical_argument_graph: Node A: Risk Factors in 10-Ks are compact, informative signals for future volatility (motivation anchored in Dyer et al. and prior work).
Node B: Existing lexicon-based methods (Kogan 2009; Wang 2013; Tsai 2014) provide baselines for volatility prediction using 10-K content.
Node C: Embedding-augmented IR term-weighting (Eq.3; t̂cdi) can transfer retrieval improvements to sentiment signal extraction by capturing semantically related terms.
Edge B->C: Prior lexicon-expansion (Tsai & Wang) motivates further embedding-based weighting rather than mere expansion.
Node D: Implement Lex and LexExt (Loughran-McDonald plus top-20 related terms from Word2Vec trained on corpus).
Node E: Apply weighting schemes (TC, TF, TFIDF, BM25) and their embedding-augmented variants (hats); reduce via PCA(400); learn with SVM-RBF.
Edge C,D->E: Embedding augmentation feeds into term weights used in the supervised model.
Node F: Market features (current volatility, GARCH, sector one-hot) provide orthogonal predictive signal.
Node G: Fusion strategies (early fusion, stacking, MKL) combine text and market signals; stacking (70/30 split) claimed best trade-off.
Edge E,F->G: Text and market base models are inputs to fusion.
Node H: Concept drift analysis (centroid cosine similarities, r2 by dropping older years) shows clusters and motivates using 2012–2015 subset.
Edge H->Dataset: Dataset restricted to 2012–2015 (3892 reports) based on drift argument.

Node I (Claims): (i) Embedding-augmented BM25 (B̂M25) achieves higher text-only r2 than baselines; (ii) Text+Market with stacking improves further and stabilizes long-term forecasts; (iii) Sector-specific models underperform general model due to small per-sector samples.
Edges E,G,H->I: The experimental pipeline produces the reported performance numbers supporting claims.
Critical dependency K: Word2Vec training on 'all reports' and PCA/hyperparameter selections — if K introduces leakage or interacts with evaluation improperly, claims I may be overstated.
Break point L: Risk Factors extraction heuristics — if extraction noisy, text features may be misrepresentative and performance gains unstable.

Verification nodes: need for (a) temporal isolation in embedding training, (b) statistical tests on r2/MSE differences, (c) sensitivity analyses for threshold/ PCA/stacking split/SVM hyperparameters, (d) ground-truth evaluation of Risk Factors extraction.

References to Rekabsaz et al. for threshold choice.

strengths.title: Clear pipeline linking IR advances to financial sentiment extraction
strengths.description: The manuscript traces a coherent path from embedding-augmented IR term-weighting methods (Eq.3) through lexicon application, PCA reduction, and SVM regression to yield measurable prediction improvements.
evidence: Section 4.1 defines embedding-augmented t̂cdi and extends standard weighting schemes.
Tables 1–2 show numeric improvements and the text explains the pipeline choices.

strengths.title: Comprehensive empirical comparisons across methods and fusion strategies
strengths.description: Authors compare multiple weighting schemes (standard and augmented), multiple fusion approaches (early, stacking, MKL), and prior baselines, enabling relative assessment of contributions.
evidence: Table 1 reports weighting schemes and fusion comparisons; Table 2 includes reproduced baselines (Wang 2013; Tsai 2014; GARCH).
Figures 2 and 3 analyze horizon and sector effects.

strengths.title: Examination of temporal drift and justification of dataset selection
strengths.description: The paper does not blindly pool all available years but provides an empirical analysis (centroid cosine similarities and r2 trends) motivating focus on recent years for modeling.
evidence: Figure 1a shows year-cluster similarities; Figure 1b shows r2 improving when older years are dropped, leading to 2012–2015 subset selection.

strengths.title: Sectoral analysis revealing interpretable term differences
strengths.description: By training linear models without PCA the authors illustrate term-level coefficients that clarify sector-specific senses (e.g., 'fire' in energy), supporting qualitative domain insights.

Figures 3 and Table 3 provide per-sector performance and sizes.

concerns.title: Potential temporal leakage from embedding training
concerns.description: Word2Vec is trained on 'the corpus of all the reports' including test-year reports; this can leak test-set linguistic information into training, inflating measured gains of embedding-augmented weighting.
evidence: Section 4.1: 'Word2Vec model, built on the corpus of all the reports.'
Shared uncertainty flags note temporal leakage as a central concern.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Retrain Word2Vec within proper folds or using only training-year reports for each experiment; report results both with and without whole-corpus training to quantify leakage effect.

concerns.title: Insufficient reporting of Risk Factors extraction quality
concerns.description: Risk Factors section extraction is done via term-matching heuristics but no precision/recall or manual inspection statistics are provided; noisy extraction could bias or obscure the true effect of textual features.
evidence: Section 5: 'We extract the Risk Factors section using term matching heuristics.' No further extraction-validation details present in main text.
Chaining notes emphasize downstream reviewers should verify extraction first.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide annotated subset evaluation (precision/recall/F1) of the Risk Factors extraction heuristics, list extraction patterns used, and discuss failure modes; if noisy, consider more robust section parsing (e.g., regex anchors with manual checks).

concerns.title: Lack of statistical testing and variability reporting
concerns.description: Reported r2 and MSE are point estimates (averages over CV) without fold-level variances, confidence intervals, or statistical tests comparing methods; effect sizes may not be robust.
evidence: Tables 1–2 present averages only; no standard deviations, p-values, or paired tests described.
Uncertainty flags note missing significance testing.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report fold-level metrics, standard errors, and perform paired tests (e.g., Wilcoxon signed-rank or paired t-test on per-fold r2) to establish significance of improvements.

concerns.title: Ad-hoc hyperparameter and pipeline choices without sensitivity analysis
concerns.description: Key choices—similarity threshold 0.70, top-20 expansion, PCA dim=400, SVM RBF with C=1 and ε=0.1, stacking 70/30 split—are stated but not ablated or justified quantitatively; rankings between methods may depend on these.
evidence: Section 4.1 and 4.3 list these choices; shared analysis flags lack of tuning details.
No reported sensitivity experiments across thresholds or PCA dims in main text.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include ablation tables varying threshold (e.g., 0.6–0.9), PCA dims (e.g., 100/400/1000), SVM gamma and C, top-k expansion sizes, and stacking split strategies (out-of-fold stacking) to demonstrate robustness.

concerns.title: Insufficient control for company-level leakage in CV
concerns.description: Multiple reports per company across years exist; 5-fold CV may place reports from same company in both train and test folds, inflating performance if company-specific patterns exist.
evidence: C10 notes 3892 reports for 1323 companies; Section 6.2 CV described but no mention of company-grouped splits.
Chaining notes explicitly highlight company-level leakage risk.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run grouped CV where all reports of a company are in one fold, or report experiments with temporal train/test splits disallowing future reports, and compare results.

concerns.title: MKL comparison may be under-tuned or computationally constrained
concerns.description: MKL (mklaren) is said to underperform stacking and early fusion in reported results, but MKL hyperparameters and kernel tuning are not detailed; conclusions about fusion hierarchy may be premature.
evidence: Section 4.3: mklaren used for MKL; Table 1 shows MKL r2 lower than stacking.
Shared analysis notes MKL computational constraints may affect relative performance.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide MKL hyperparameters, kernel bandwidth tuning, and report whether performance changes when allocating more computation or tuning; consider out-of-fold meta-features for stacking comparisons.

concerns.title: Outlier filtering of labels may bias evaluation
concerns.description: Removing volatility labels beyond mean ±3σ can exclude meaningful high-volatility events and artificially improve r2; impact on tail predictive ability is not assessed.
evidence: Section 5: explicit statement of outlier filtering but no sensitivity analysis.
Uncertainty flags mention tail-event removal affecting real-world relevance.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report results with and without outlier filtering, and provide separate metrics for tail-event prediction (e.g., top-decile volatility) to assess practical performance.

concerns.title: Ambiguity in Word2Vec training provenance and parameters
concerns.description: Word2Vec parameters (vector size, window, epochs, negative sampling) and corpus splits are omitted, reducing reproducibility and making embedding quality and expansion choices unverifiable.
evidence: Section 4.1 notes Word2Vec built on corpus but no hyperparameters provided.
Shared analysis lists missing Word2Vec training details as an uncertainty.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add Word2Vec configuration and training scripts or exact parameters in supplementary materials; state whether embeddings were re-trained per CV fold or globally.

Risk Factors extraction via heuristics without validation -> possible noisy inputs.

Hyperparameter choices (similarity threshold, top-20 expansion, PCA dimension, SVM gamma) lack ablation -> sensitivity unknown.

alternative_interpretations: Apparent improvements from embedding-augmented weighting could arise from leakage where embeddings encode future/test vocabulary patterns (if trained on all reports), rather than genuine generalizable semantic augmentation.

Stacking gains over MKL/early fusion may reflect differences in effective model capacity or tuning regimes (stacking meta-model benefits from particular SVM hyperparameters) rather than an inherent superiority of late fusion for this task.

Improved performance on the 2012–2015 subset might reflect regime-specific properties (e.g., macroeconomic conditions) rather than intrinsic superiority of recent reports; generalizability to other periods could be limited.
Sector-specific underperformance may be due to naive per-sector modeling choices (no transfer learning or hierarchy) rather than a fundamental lack of sector-specific signal.
transparency_notes: Key implementation details (Word2Vec training params, exact Risk Factors extraction heuristics, PCA selection traces, SVM gamma tuning, MKL parameters) are missing from the main text and are necessary for replication.
The authors state some implementation details are in supplementary material (e.g., GARCH) — important reproducibility items should be present or explicitly linked.
Reported metrics are means over CV folds but per-fold values, standard deviations, and statistical tests are not shown; adding these would improve transparency and inferential validity.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The method adapts recent IR embedding-augmented term-weighting to financial sentiment for volatility prediction — this is a domain transfer with plausible novelty; however, empirical validity depends on rigorous controls for leakage and robust sensitivity analyses. Novelty (lack of close analogs) should not be conflated with correctness without these controls.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If Word2Vec embeddings are trained only on past (training-fold) reports, and embedding augmentation still improves r2, then the method's gains are likely genuine and generalizable.
If company-level grouped CV produces similar improvements, then gains are not due to company-specific leakage.
If ablations show stability across similarity thresholds, PCA dims, and SVM hyperparameters, then the reported ranking (B̂M25 > BM25 etc.) is robust.
If Risk Factors extraction is validated (high precision/recall), then text-signal claims are supported; otherwise, improvements may be dataset-artifact-driven.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The core technical idea (embedding-augmented weighting) originates in IR literature (Rekabsaz et al.); applying it to financial lexicon weighting for volatility prediction is an adaptation rather than a wholly new algorithm, but the applied domain and the empirical gains provide practical novelty.
evidence: Section 4.1 cites Rekabsaz et al. for the augmentation approach and adapts Eq.3 to sentiment weighting.
Tsai & Wang (2014) used embeddings for lexicon expansion, but this paper uses augmentation of weights (a different, though related, mechanism).
uncertainty_flags: Degree of novelty depends on whether embedding-augmentation was previously applied to sentiment-weighting in finance; the paper argues not, but literature overlap with Tsai & Wang is close.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Reported r2 increases (text-only and text+market) and stability across horizons indicate practical utility for volatility forecasting, contingent on robustness checks; the sectoral and drift analyses add applied insights.
evidence: Table 2: Our method Text+Market r2=0.527 vs prior best ~0.499.
Figure 2 shows more stable long-horizon performance when text is included.
uncertainty_flags: Practical impact depends on confirming absence of leakage, robustness to alternative splits, and performance on unfiltered labels/tail events.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Missing exact preprocessing and training parameter details (embedding and MKL hyperparameters, Risk Factors extraction heuristics) impede independent replication.
evidence: Multiple implementation choices stated without full parameters (Word2Vec, PCA experiments, SVM gamma).
Some implementation details moved to supplementary or not provided.
uncertainty_flags: Supplementary might contain some missing details; however, main text should summarize critical reproducibility parameters.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately confident that the core empirical pattern (embedding-augmented weighting can help volatility prediction and stacking fusion often improves combined Text+Market performance) holds within the presented experimental setup. However, major methodological issues (possible temporal/company-level leakage, lack of statistical testing, missing extraction validation and hyperparameter sensitivity) materially reduce confidence in the generalizability of the effect; hence a broad CI reflecting this uncertainty.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: Reconstructed reasoning: The paper posits that Risk Factors (Item 1A) of 10-Ks contain predictive signal for future stock volatility. It extracts Risk Factor text via term-matching heuristics, stems, and computes lexicon-based features (Lex and LexExt). It augments traditional IR term-weighting schemes (TC, TF, TFIDF, BM25) by expanding lexicon-term counts with similar words identified via Word2Vec similarity (threshold 0.70) and substitutes these augmented counts into weighting formulae (Eq.3) to form T̂C, T̂F, T̂FIDF, B̂M25. High-dimensional sparse vectors are reduced with PCA (chosen dimension=400). SVM-RBF (C=1, ε=0.1) is trained to predict realized volatility aggregated per quarter; evaluation uses 5-fold CV on a temporally filtered subset (reports 2012–2015, N=3892). Market features (current volatility, GARCH, sector one-hot) are separately modeled and fused with text using early fusion, MKL (mklaren), and stacking (70/30 train split for base/meta). Main empirical results: embedding-augmented BM25 (B̂M25) yields higher r2 than prior lexicon/SVM baselines; stacking improves Text+Market r2 over other fusion methods; recent-year subset outperforms older pooled data (claimed concept drift); sector-specific models underperform a pooled general model (attributed to limited per-sector data). Key operational choices (Word2Vec training on all reports, similarity threshold 0.70, PCA=400, fixed SVM hyperparameters, outlier filtering mean±3σ) underpin results but are incompletely specified in main text and pose reproducibility and validity risks. The reported improvements lack formal significance testing and full sensitivity analyses (hyperparameters, temporal leakage, extraction accuracy, stacking stability).
logical_argument_graph: A1: Risk Factors provide predictive signal for future volatility => justify focusing on Item 1A.
Data extraction pipeline: download 10-Ks (2006–2015) -> extract Risk Factors via term-matching heuristics -> clean & Porter-stem.
Create lexicon features: Lex (Loughran-McDonald) and LexExt (expand via Word2Vec trained on corpus).
Augment term counts using embedding similarity: t̂cdi(t) = tcdi(t) + sum_{t' in R(t)} sim(t,t') tcdi(t') with threshold 0.70 (Eq.3).
Compute IR weighting schemes (TC, TF, TFIDF, BM25) and their augmented variants (with hat) replacing tcdi with t̂cdi.
Dimensionality reduction via PCA; pick 400 dims after preliminary sweep.
Train SVM-RBF (C=1, ε=0.1) on PC features to predict realized volatility labels y1..y8 (focus on first-year mean over first 4 quartiles).
Evaluate on 2012–2015 subset using 5-fold CV; compare text-only, market-only (GARCH/current vol), and fusion methods (early, MKL, stacking).
Observe embedding-augmented BM25 (B̂M25) outperforms prior baselines and un-augmented variants; stacking with B̂M25 + market features yields best reported Text+Market r2.
Temporal analysis: centroid similarity and rolling exclusion of older years show improved r2 when restricted to 2012–2015 => argue concept drift warrants recent subset.
Sector analysis: per-sector models underperform pooled model; controlled sampling suggests sample size explains underperformance.

identified_claims.claim_label: embedding-augmented IR improves text-only volatility prediction
identified_claims.claim_text: Word-embedding-augmented IR term-weighting schemes (extended TC, TF, TFIDF, BM25: denoted with hats) applied to the Loughran-McDonald lexicon (Lex, LexExt) produce substantially better volatility prediction from 10-K Risk Factors than prior lexicon/SVM baselines (Wang et al. 2013; Tsai and Wang 2014).

Table 1: B̂M25 (Text r2=0.439) higher than variants and text baselines.
Table 2: Our method (Text) r2=0.439 vs reproduced Wang (2013) 0.345 and Tsai (2014) 0.395.

Details of Word2Vec training (params) not provided; embeddings trained on all reports possibly include test data (temporal leakage).
Improvements may depend on PCA=400 and fixed SVM hyperparameters; sensitivity not shown.

identified_claims.claim_label: stacking fusion improves combined Text+Market prediction
identified_claims.claim_text: Combining textual sentiment features with market-derived features (current volatility, GARCH, sector one-hot) via stacking yields further improvements in r2 and lower MSE compared to either modality alone and compared to early fusion and MKL in these experiments.

Figure 2a shows Text+Market curve above others across quartiles.

Meta-learner choice (SVM-RBF, same hyperparams) may advantage or disadvantage methods unequally.

identified_claims.claim_label: temporal concept drift and recent-data superiority
identified_claims.claim_text: Concept drift is present in 10-K reports across years; using more recent subsets (2012–2015) produces better predictive performance than pooling older years.

Figure 1b: r2 improves as older years are dropped, authors choose 2012–2015 subset.

Results shown for 2012–2015 subset only; external validity for other periods not shown.

strengths.title: Comprehensive comparative experimental setup
strengths.description: Authors compare multiple weighting schemes, Lex vs LexExt, and three fusion methods (early, MKL, stacking) with both r2 and MSE reported, enabling relative evaluation.

concerns.title: Potential temporal leakage via Word2Vec trained on entire corpus
concerns.description: Word2Vec is trained 'on the corpus of all the reports' and used to create LexExt and R(t). If embeddings include test-year reports, similarity augmentation may indirectly leak test information to training features and inflate reported improvements.

concerns.title: Underspecified Risk Factors extraction and no extraction quality assessment
concerns.description: Extraction of Item 1A Risk Factors uses term-matching heuristics but paper provides no precision/recall, manual checks, or examples; mis-extraction can introduce noisy or irrelevant text affecting downstream features and claims.

concerns.title: No statistical testing for reported performance differences
concerns.description: Tables report r2 and MSE differences across methods but lack paired statistical tests (e.g., paired t, Wilcoxon) across CV folds to establish significance of improvements (e.g., B̂M25 vs Tsai 2014 or stacking vs MKL).

concerns.description: PCA dimension=400 and SVM parameters (C, ε, RBF gamma) are stated as chosen from initial experiments, but no validation curves, search ranges, or interaction analyses provided. These choices can materially affect relative ranking of methods.

Shared Analysis flags sensitivity risk.

concerns.description: Stacking uses a single 70/30 split for base/meta training; no out-of-fold stacking or multiple split trials to assess variance. As stacking outperforms MKL and early fusion, its stability must be demonstrated.

concerns.title: Potential company-level leakage across CV folds

concerns.title: MKL implementation opacity

No paired statistical tests or per-fold variances reported for claimed improvements.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper argues that focused sentiment features extracted from 10-K Risk Factors, when computed using embedding-augmented IR term-weighting schemes (notably an extended BM25 denoted B̂M25), produce stronger volatility forecasts than prior lexicon/SVM baselines. The authors operationalize this by: (1) extracting Risk Factors text, (2) applying finance lexicons (Lex and an embedding-expanded LexExt), (3) computing standard and embedding-augmented IR weights (Eq.3, using Word2Vec similarity threshold 0.70), (4) reducing sparsity with PCA (chosen dimension 400), (5) training SVM-RBF regressors, and (6) combining text and market features via stacking (70/30 split) with MKL and early fusion as comparisons. They justify restricting the main evaluation to a 2012–2015 subset on the basis of centroid cosine-similarity and improved r2 when older years are dropped (claimed concept drift). Empirical results on 5-fold CV show B̂M25 (text-only) improving r2 over reproduced baselines (Wang 2013, Tsai 2014) and further gains when stacking text with market features (Text+Market r2 increases). Sectoral analysis shows heterogeneous term importance but sector-specific models underperform a pooled model — attributed to limited per-sector training data. The paper thus claims incremental methodological novelty (embedding-augmented IR term-weighting applied to long-form financial texts) and several empirical findings about fusion, temporal drift, and sector size effects. Key uncertainties affecting novelty and interpretation include potential temporal leakage (Word2Vec trained on entire corpus), heuristic Risk Factors extraction, limited hyperparameter reporting (Word2Vec, PCA selection, SVM gamma), absence of statistical significance testing, and the choice to focus results on a recent-year subset.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: Reconstructed reasoning: The authors posit that the Risk Factors section of 10-Ks contains predictive information about future volatility. They operationalize this by (1) extracting Risk Factors (heuristic term-matching), (2) representing sentiment via Loughran-McDonald lexicon (Lex) and an expanded version (LexExt) obtained from Word2Vec trained on the report corpus, (3) computing IR-style term-weighting schemes (TC, TF, TFIDF, BM25) and their embedding-augmented variants (hat-versions) where each lexicon term's weight t̂cdi includes counts of similar words weighted by cosine similarity (threshold 0.70), (4) reducing the high-dimensional lexicon-weight vectors by PCA (chosen dimension = 400), (5) training SVR with RBF kernel (C=1.0, ε=0.1) to predict quarter-aggregated realized volatility labels, and (6) combining textual features with market features (current volatility, GARCH, sector one-hot) using fusion strategies; stacking (70/30 internal split) is recommended. Empirically, on a curated 2012–2015 subset (3892 reports; 1323 companies), embedding-augmented BM25 (B̂M25) yields the best text-only r2 and stacking Text+Market improves further (reported Text only r2≈0.439, Text+Market r2≈0.527). The paper argues concept drift across years (centroid cosine clusters), motivating use of 2012–2015 subset; sector analyses indicate heterogeneous term importances but sector-specific models underperform general models due to limited per-sector sample sizes. The manuscript combines IR embedding-augmentation with financial lexica and a practical fusion pipeline and reports that these methodological choices materially increase r2 over reproduced baselines. Key uncertainties remain about extraction reliability, temporal leakage (Word2Vec trained on full corpus), hyperparameter search reporting (PCA, SVM gamma, Word2Vec), statistical testing, and the sensitivity of stacking and MKL settings.

Reference to Tsai & Wang (2014) methodology for expansion.

Top-20 choice and later similarity threshold interaction not fully justified.
Possible leakage if Word2Vec sees test-year reports.

evidence: Section 6.1: explicit statement that 2012–2015 subset has 3892 reports and 1323 companies.

strengths.title: Well-motivated adaptation of embedding-augmented IR
strengths.description: Applying IR term-weighting extended by word-embedding similarity to lexicon-based sentiment transforms sparse lexicon counts into semantically richer signals appropriate for long 10-K texts.
evidence: Section 4.1 Eq.3 and textual justification referencing Rekabsaz et al.
Quantitative improvements for B̂M25 over BM25 and other schemes in Table 1.

strengths.title: Comprehensive experimental comparisons
strengths.description: The paper reproduces prior baselines, compares multiple weighting schemes, fusion strategies (early/stacking/MKL), and analyzes sector and temporal effects.
evidence: Tables 1–2 compare proposed method with Wang (2013) and Tsai (2014).
Experiments include fusion comparisons, time-split scenarios (2013/2014/2015), and per-sector analyses (Figures 2–3).

strengths.title: Attention to temporal drift and dataset curation
strengths.description: Authors detect multi-year clusters in report text and explicitly justify restricting experiments to a recent, coherent subset (2012–2015) to reduce concept-drift noise.
evidence: Figure 1a centroid similarity heatmap and Figure 1b showing r2 improvement when dropping older years.
Textual rationale in Section 6.1.

strengths.title: Practical fusion pipeline for combining text and market signals
strengths.description: Demonstrates a computationally practical stacking approach that yields stronger combined performance than alternatives in these experiments.
evidence: Section 4.3 stacking description and Table 1 showing stacking best among fusion methods.
Figure 2a showing Text+Market improved stability over longer horizons.

concerns.title: Temporal leakage from training Word2Vec on full corpus
concerns.description: Word2Vec and LexExt appear to be trained/constructed using the entire corpus (all reports), which includes test-year documents. This can leak future-test information into features (semantic expansion and similarity patterns), artificially inflating reported gains for embedding-augmented schemes.
evidence: Section 4.1: 'Word2Vec ... built on the corpus of all the reports.'
Uncertainty flags in shared analysis noting potential temporal leakage.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Retrain Word2Vec within strictly separated training folds or using only pre-publication data for each train/test split; report results with fold-wise embedding training and compare to full-corpus embeddings.

concerns.title: Unspecified Risk Factors extraction accuracy
concerns.description: Risk Factors sections are extracted by term-matching heuristics but the extraction method and its precision/recall are not reported. Inconsistent or noisy extraction could alter both lexicon counts and embedding similarity contexts.
evidence: Section 5: 'We extract the Risk Factors section using term matching heuristics.' No extraction evaluation given.
Shared analysis notes heuristic extraction details not provided.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide algorithmic details for extraction, annotate a held-out subset with human-labeled Item 1A boundaries, and report extraction precision/recall; re-run key experiments on verified extractions.

concerns.title: Insufficient hyperparameter and sensitivity reporting
concerns.description: Key choices (Word2Vec hyperparameters, similarity-threshold 0.70 sensitivity, PCA 400 selection procedure, SVM gamma search, MKL and stacking meta-learner choices) lack detailed reporting or sensitivity analyses; results may hinge on these.
evidence: Section 4.1 states 400 dims was optimum but gives no experimental curve or metric.
Similarity threshold 0.70 adopted from Rekabsaz but corpus-specific sensitivity not shown.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add ablation/sensitivity plots: r2 vs PCA dims, r2 vs similarity threshold, results with Word2Vec variants (sizes/windows), and SVM grid search (including gamma). Document mklaren and stacking meta-model hyperparameters.

concerns.title: No statistical tests or uncertainty quantification on r2 improvements
concerns.description: The paper reports point estimates of r2/MSE but does not provide significance testing (paired tests across folds or bootstrap CIs) to establish whether the improvements over reproduced baselines are robust.
evidence: Tables show mean r2 and MSE but no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or p-values are reported.
Shared analysis flagged missing statistical significance tests.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report standard deviations over folds, paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests comparing methods per fold, and/or bootstrap confidence intervals for r2 differences.

concerns.title: Potential company-level leakage in cross-validation
concerns.description: Multiple reports per company across years (1323 companies, 3892 reports) could place documents from the same company in both train and test folds, producing optimistic performance via company-specific signals.
evidence: Shared analysis notes that fold counts and company-level leakage handling are not fully detailed.
Dataset description mentions multiple reports per company but no company-wise fold partitioning rule given.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify cross-validation partitioning rules and, if not already done, perform company-wise grouped CV (i.e., all reports of a company in a single fold). Recalculate main metrics under grouped CV and report differences.

concerns.title: Label filtering of volatility extremes may bias evaluation
concerns.description: Removing volatility values more than ±3σ from the mean can exclude tail events that are precisely the most consequential targets for volatility forecasting and may artificially raise r2 by truncating variance.
evidence: Section 5: 'We filter the volatility values greater/smaller than the mean plus/minus three times the standard deviation...'
Shared analysis notes potential impact on tail-event performance and real-world relevance.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report experiments with and without outlier filtering, or use robust metrics; provide distributional plots of labels pre/post filtering and quantify how many/which reports are excluded (e.g., crisis periods).

comparable_works.source_trace: Cited in Section 4.1 as direct methodological predecessor

comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: mklaren chosen for computational tractability; current paper uses mklaren but tuning/details not fully reported.

uncertainty_flags: Word2Vec training on full corpus may cause temporal leakage affecting LexExt and embedding-augmentation.
Risk Factors extraction relies on heuristics; extraction quality (precision/recall) not reported.
No statistical tests (CI/p-values) shown for r2/MSE differences between methods.
PCA dimension choice (400) and SVM hyperparameters (gamma) lack reproducibility details and sensitivity analyses.
Cross-validation may not be grouped by company — potential optimistic leakage if reports from same company appear in train and test folds.
Outlier removal (±3σ) could truncate important tail examples altering model evaluation.
alternative_interpretations: Reported embedding-augmentation gains may partly stem from temporal leakage via Word2Vec exposure to test documents rather than pure methodological improvement.

Improved performance when restricting to 2012–2015 could reflect a regime where market-text correlation was stronger (macro conditions) rather than purely reduced noise from concept drift; results may not generalize to other regimes.

Stacking gains might be due to particular train/validation split and meta-learner regularization rather than an intrinsic superiority of late fusion; MKL performance could improve with different hyperparameterization.
PCA=400 and fixed SVM settings could advantage some weighting schemes; ranking of methods might change under different dimensionality reduction or tuned learners.
transparency_notes: Provide Word2Vec training parameters (vector dim, window, min-count, epochs, architecture CBOW/skip-gram) and whether embeddings were trained fold-wise or on full corpus.
Release Risk Factors extraction code and an annotated validation set with extraction metrics (precision/recall/IoU for section boundaries).
Report cross-validation partitioning policy (standard CV vs company-grouped CV) and exact train/test counts per fold/year.
Document PCA selection experiments (plots of r2 vs dims, variance explained) and SVM hyperparameter grid search including RBF gamma values.
Give mklaren/MKL hyperparameters and stacking meta-learner details (regularization, kernel for meta SVM), and number of random seeds used.
Report counts of volatility values removed by ±3σ filtering and results without filtering.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The relative paucity of identical prior applications (embedding-augmented IR weighting applied to lexicon-based sentiment in long regulatory filings for volatility prediction) should be seen as a potential innovation signal; however, novelty alone does not guarantee correctness — empirical rigor (no leakage, reproducible hyperparameters, and statistical validation) is required to establish validity.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If Word2Vec is trained only on temporally prior documents (no exposure to test-year text) and company-level leakage is controlled, embedding-augmented weighting still improves r2 — then method likely generalizes.
If PCA and SVM hyperparameters are robust across folds and improvements persist across multiple time regimes (e.g., out-of-sample years beyond 2015), the idea scales and is impactful.

If Risk Factors extraction accuracy is high (verified on human labels) and embedding-augmentation improves retrieval-weighting semantics without introducing noise from rare-word similarity, the approach will be valuable for other long-form regulatory texts.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper transfers a relatively new IR technique (embedding-augmented term weighting) into the domain of lexicon-based financial sentiment for long-form documents — an application niche with limited direct precedent. This cross-pollination is conceptually novel and has potential to change how lexicon signals are aggregated in long-document financial NLP.
evidence: Section 4.1 cites Rekabsaz et al. for embedding-augmented weighting but applies it to lexicon sentiment instead of retrieval tasks.
Quantitative gains reported vs established baselines (Tables 1–2).
uncertainty_flags: Effectiveness depends on removing temporal/company-level leakage and demonstrating robustness across time periods and hyperparameters.

novelty_lenses.rationale: From the perspective of the existing finance-NLP literature (Tsai & Wang 2014; Wang et al. 2013), the paper can be read as a systematic engineering and evaluation advance: lexicon expansion and SVM pipelines were known; the paper refines weighting and fusion and reports improved metrics. Thus, absent rigorous controls for leakage and sensitivity, gains might reflect careful tuning and dataset selection rather than a fundamentally new class of models.
evidence: Tsai & Wang (2014) already used Word2Vec for lexicon expansion; this paper's core novelty is in weighting aggregation (embedding-augmented IR) and fusion engineering.
Some methodological choices (PCA, fixed SVM params, subset selection) are standard tuning steps rather than conceptual leaps.
uncertainty_flags: Distinguishing disruptive novelty from incremental tuning requires rigorous ablations, fold-wise embedding training, and grouped CV to rule out alternative explanations.

confidence_interval.rationale: I have moderate confidence in the paper's reported direction of improvement (embedding-augmented weighting and stacking appear promising) because results are consistent and the idea is plausible. However, methodological uncertainties (potential temporal/company-level leakage, missing hyperparameter/sensitivity details, and absent statistical tests) materially reduce confidence in the magnitude and generality of claims. The interval reflects meaningful chance that some reported gains shrink or lose significance once these issues are controlled.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper adapts embedding-augmented IR term-weighting schemes (extended TC/TF/TFIDF/BM25 using Word2Vec similarity; Eq.3) on Risk Factors sections of SEC 10-Ks to predict realized volatility. The pipeline: heuristic extraction of Item 1A Risk Factors, stemming, lexicon features (Loughran-McDonald Lex and expanded LexExt via Word2Vec trained on all reports), compute standard and augmented term-weightings, PCA (chosen 400 dims), SVM-RBF regression (C=1.0, ε=0.1), and fusion with market features (current volatility, GARCH, sector one-hot) via early fusion, MKL (mklaren), and stacking (70/30 split). Main empirical claims are (a) embedding-augmented BM25 (B̂M25) improves text-only r2 over reproduced baselines (Wang 2013, Tsai 2014), (b) stacking Text+Market yields further r2 gains and more stable long-horizon forecasts, (c) concept drift across years justifies restricting experiments to 2012–2015 (N=3892 reports), and (d) sector-specific models currently underperform pooled general model due to small per-sector sample sizes. The manuscript reports r2 and MSE comparisons (Tables 1–2) but omits fold-level variance, significance tests, and several operational details (Word2Vec params, exact extraction heuristic, SVM gamma search, PCA selection experiments). Key methodological risks that could explain or inflate reported gains are: potential temporal leakage from training Word2Vec on the entire corpus (including test reports), lack of validated Risk Factors extraction, fixed SVM hyperparameters without sensitivity ablation, stacking split sensitivity, and outlier filtering of labels (mean ±3σ) possibly removing meaningful tail events. Where evidence is present in the paper (reported r2 numbers, equations, figures), the claims are supported conditionally — i.e., valid under the reported pipeline and dataset choices — but the results' robustness and external generalizability remain uncertain until the above risks are addressed with ablations and leakage controls.
logical_argument_graph: A1: Risk Factors (Item 1A) are informative for future volatility -> justify focusing on Risk Factors (Introduction; Dyer et al. citation).
A2: Extract Risk Factors via heuristics and preprocess -> produce document corpus (Section 5).
A3: Compute lexicon-based features (Lex, LexExt) and embed-augment term counts using Word2Vec similarity (Eq.3) -> produce enriched term-weight vectors (Section 4.1).
A4: Reduce dimensionality via PCA (400 dims chosen) and train SVM-RBF -> produce volatility predictions (Sections 4.1, 6.2).
A5: Evaluate on 2012–2015 subset (selected due to centroid similarity and r2 improvement when dropping older years) using 5-fold CV -> claim improved r2 for B̂M25 vs. baselines (Figure1, Table1/2).
A6: Combine text and market features via stacking/MKL/early fusion -> stacking yields best Text+Market r2 (Table1).
A7: Sector-level analysis: per-sector term importance exists but sector-specific models underperform general model due to small per-sector sample sizes (Section 6.3, Figures 2c,3).

Conclusion: Embedding-augmented IR weighting (esp. B̂M25) plus stacking with market features materially improves first-year volatility r2 over reproduced lexicon baselines, with added long-term stability from text features.

identified_claims.claim_label: embedding-augmented IR improves text-only volatility prediction
identified_claims.claim_text: Word-embedding-augmented IR term-weighting schemes (extended TC, TF, TFIDF, BM25: denoted with hats) applied to the Loughran-McDonald lexicon (Lex, LexExt) produce substantially better volatility prediction from 10-K Risk Factors than prior lexicon/SVM baselines (Wang et al. 2013; Tsai and Wang 2014).
evidence: Definition of augmented counts t̂cdi(t) in Eq.3 and threshold 0.70 for similar words (Section 4.1).
Table 2: Our method (text-only) r2=0.439 vs Wang (2013) 0.345 and Tsai (2014) 0.395 (Section 6.2).
Text: 'In general, the extended schemes (with hat) improve upon their normal forms.' (Section 6.2)
uncertainty_flags: Word2Vec trained on entire corpus (all years) may include test-year reports -> potential temporal leakage inflating performance (A2/A9).
No statistical significance tests or fold-level variance reported; unclear whether observed r2 differences are robust.
Hyperparameters for Word2Vec (vector size, window, epochs) and threshold choice not tuned/sensitively reported; possible dependency on those choices.

identified_claims.claim_label: stacking fusion improves combined Text+Market prediction
identified_claims.claim_text: Combining textual sentiment features with market-derived features (current volatility, GARCH) via stacking yields further improvements in r2 and lower MSE compared to either modality alone and compared to early fusion and MKL in these experiments.
evidence: Description of stacking (70/30 split) in Section 4.3.
Table 1: B̂M25 Text-only r2=0.439 -> Text+Market stacking r2=0.527, MSE improved 0.132->0.111.
Table 1: Stacking r2=0.527 vs MKL r2=0.488 and Early Fusion r2=0.473 (Section 6.2).
uncertainty_flags: Stacking uses a fixed 70/30 internal split; no sensitivity analysis reported (split randomness, meta-learner choice).
MKL hyperparameters and mklaren approximation details not fully described; computational shortcuts might affect MKL performance.
Potential company-level leakage in CV could advantage fusion if same companies appear across folds in different roles.

identified_claims.claim_label: temporal concept drift and recent-data superiority
identified_claims.claim_text: Concept drift is present in 10-K reports across years; using more recent subsets (2012–2015) produces better predictive performance than pooling older years.
evidence: Figure 1a: centroid cosine similarity heatmap shows three clusters of years.
Figure 1b: r2 improves when dropping older years from training (2006->2015 to 2012->2015).
Text: selection of 2012–2015 subset (3892 reports) justified by coherence (Section 6.1).
uncertainty_flags: Drift analysis uses centroid cosine similarity of Tsai&Wang features; alternative drift measures not reported.
Performance improvement when dropping older years could be due to label distribution changes or sample-size effects rather than intrinsic concept drift.
No formal statistical or temporal holdout tests to quantify drift effect or to show generalization beyond 2015.

identified_claims.claim_label: general model outperforms sector-specific models given current data sizes
identified_claims.claim_text: Sectoral reports display distinct risk-related language; however, training sector-specific models on the current dataset sizes does not beat a general model trained on all sectors (likely due to limited per-sector data).
evidence: Figure 2c shows per-sector r2 differences; Figures 3a/3b show sector-specific models underperforming general model.
Table 3 reports per-sector sample counts (e.g., finance 847, tech 408).
Sector-agnostic equal-size sampling experiment approximates sample-size effect (Section 6.3).
uncertainty_flags: Sector-agnostic sampling experiment demonstrates sample-size effect but lacks statistical testing to quantify significance.
Sector labels (NASDAQ categories) may be coarse; intra-sector heterogeneity not controlled.
Alternative approaches (transfer learning, hierarchical modelling) not tested; conclusion limited to the tested methods.

identified_claims.claim_label: text adds long-term stability to volatility forecasts
identified_claims.claim_text: Textual features from 10-K Risk Factors provide predictive power that decays less rapidly than market-only features over longer horizons; combining text and market features produces more stable long-term volatility forecasts.
evidence: Figure 2a: market-based curves (GARCH, Market) decline more steeply across quartiles Q5–Q8 than Text or Text+Market curves.
Text in 6.2: 'the combination of the features shows more stable results in the later quartiles.'
uncertainty_flags: Curve differences shown for this dataset/time period; replication on other periods not demonstrated.
Label construction for later quarters and outlier filtering may affect apparent decay rates.
No confidence intervals or tests for the quartile-wise differences are reported.

identified_claims.claim_label: PCA and SVM hyperparameter choices
identified_claims.claim_text: PCA reduction to 400 dimensions was selected as optimal after testing 50–1000; SVM with RBF kernel, C=1.0 and epsilon=0.1 was used as learner with better performance than linear and cosine kernels.
evidence: Section 4.1: 'Our initial experiments show 400 dimension as the optimum by trying on a range of dimensions from 50 to 1000.'
Section 4.1: SVM settings C=1.0, ε=0.1; RBF chosen over linear/cosine per initial experiments.
uncertainty_flags: Details of PCA selection experiments (validation procedure, metric) not shown.
No reported search over SVM gamma or alternative C/ε; fixed parameters may advantage some feature types.
Interaction between PCA dimension and SVM hyperparameters not tested.

evidence: Section 5: description of download, HTML removal, Risk Factors extraction via heuristics, and Porter stemming.
Section 3: volatility definition (Eq.1) and per-quarter aggregation (Eq.2).
Section 5: outlier filtering mean ±3σ mentioned.
uncertainty_flags: Extraction heuristics are not detailed or validated on an annotated sample; extraction errors could introduce noise or bias.
Outlier filtering may remove economically important extremes and bias r2 upward.
Use of Yahoo prices and any adjustments (splits/dividends) not fully described; GARCH implementation deferred to supplementary material.

identified_claims.claim_label: lexicon construction and expansion
identified_claims.claim_text: The finance lexicon is Loughran & McDonald (2011) groups positive/negative/uncertain (Lex); LexExt created by adding top-20 related terms per lexicon term via Word2Vec trained on corpus of all reports (cosine similarity), mirroring Tsai & Wang (2014) expansion.
evidence: Section 4.1: explicit description of Lex and LexExt with top-20 related terms via Word2Vec trained on corpus of all reports.
References to Tsai & Wang (2014) technique.
uncertainty_flags: Word2Vec training details (model architecture, vector size, window, epochs) absent; expansion composition may vary widely with these.
Training Word2Vec on full corpus risks leakage if used across CV folds and temporal tests.
Choice of top-20 per term and possible filtering not justified with ablation.

identified_claims.claim_label: similarity threshold in embedding-augmentation
identified_claims.claim_text: When extending lexicon term counts to include similar words (Eq.3), the authors use cosine similarity threshold of 0.70 for selecting R(t), following Rekabsaz et al.
evidence: Section 4.1: 'we use the Cosine similarity function with threshold 0.70 for selecting the set R(t) of similar words.'
Citation to Rekabsaz et al. (2016/2017) for threshold justification.
uncertainty_flags: Threshold choice may not be optimal for this specific corpus; no sensitivity analysis shown.
Similarity estimates for rare words can be unreliable and may introduce noise.

identified_claims.claim_label: dataset size for final experiments
identified_claims.claim_text: Final main experiments are conducted on the 2012–2015 subset consisting of 3892 reports from 1323 companies.
evidence: Section 6.1: 'This subset ... consists of 3892 reports, belonging to 1323 companies.'
uncertainty_flags: Train/test split counts per fold and treatment of multiple reports per company across folds not specified; possible company-level leakage.
Sector/year imbalance within subset not fully reported.

strengths.title: Well-motivated adaptation of embedding-augmented IR methods to long financial texts
strengths.description: The paper clearly connects IR advances (embedding-augmented weighting) to the domain problem of extracting sentiment from long 10-K Risk Factors and justifies applying document-level augmentation rather than short-text techniques.
evidence: Introduction motivating use of Item 1A Risk Factors and referencing Rekabsaz et al.'s embedding-augmentation (Sections 1 and 4.1).
Explicit equation (Eq.3) and implementation of extended weight t̂cdi(t).

strengths.title: Comprehensive empirical comparisons and fusion exploration
strengths.description: Authors compare multiple weighting schemes (standard and embedding-augmented), lexicon expansions (Lex/LexExt), and fusion strategies (early, MKL, stacking), and report both r2 and MSE, giving a multi-angle empirical view.
evidence: Tables 1 and 2 compare weighting schemes and fusion methods; Figure 2 shows temporal quartile performance.
Use of MKL (mklaren) and stacking described and evaluated (Section 4.3, 6.2).

strengths.title: Attention to temporal dynamics and sector heterogeneity
strengths.description: Paper analyses year-wise centroid similarities to motivate restricting to recent years and performs per-sector performance and interpretability analyses (term coefficients) to explain domain differences.
evidence: Figure 1a/b supporting year clustering and r2 trend; Figures 2c and 3 explore sector differences and term-level examples (e.g., 'fire', 'beneficial').

concerns.title: Potential temporal leakage from Word2Vec trained on entire corpus
concerns.description: Word2Vec used for LexExt and for the embedding-augmented counts t̂cdi(t) is trained on the whole corpus (all reports across years). If representations include test reports, similarity-based expansions may leak future information into training and inflate reported performance.
evidence: Section 4.1: 'Word2Vec ... built on the corpus of all the reports' (explicit).
Shared analysis and prior reviewers flag temporal leakage as high-risk.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Retrain Word2Vec within strictly separated training data for each CV fold and for temporal holdouts (train only on past years for forward tests); re-run key experiments (text-only and Text+Market stacking) and report the difference in r2/MSE.

concerns.title: Unvalidated heuristic extraction of Risk Factors section
concerns.description: Risk Factors (Item 1A) extraction is done by term-matching heuristics but no precision/recall or human-annotated validation is reported. Mis-extraction (partial sections or incorrect boundaries) could add noise or systematically bias text features.
evidence: Section 5: 'We extract the Risk Factors section using term matching heuristics.' No validation metrics given.
Shared analysis notes absent extraction quality assessment.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a small annotated set (e.g., 100 reports) with human-labeled Risk Factors boundaries; report extraction precision/recall and error examples; if errors are non-trivial, refine heuristics or use supervised section extraction.

concerns.title: Lack of statistical testing and variability reporting
concerns.description: Reported r2/MSE are averages (5-fold CV), but fold-level variance, confidence intervals, or paired statistical tests between methods are missing, making it unclear whether reported improvements are statistically significant.
evidence: Tables 1–2 show point estimates without CI or p-values; prior-stage reviewers flagged absence of statistical tests.
Figures present single curves without error bands.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report per-fold r2 and MSE, add standard deviations and 95% confidence intervals; conduct paired tests (e.g., Wilcoxon signed-rank or t-test on folds) comparing B̂M25 vs best baseline and stacking vs MKL/early fusion.

concerns.title: Hyperparameter and preprocessing sensitivity underreported
concerns.description: Key choices—Word2Vec parameters (dim, window, epochs), similarity threshold (0.70), top-20 expansion, PCA dimension (400), SVM gamma/C/epsilon—are not fully explored; fixed settings may advantage certain methods and hide sensitivity.
evidence: Sections 4.1 and 5 state choices (threshold 0.70, top-20, PCA=400, C=1.0, ε=0.1) but omit search ranges, validation details, or results of selection process.
Shared analysis notes missing ablation studies.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add ablation tables: (a) Word2Vec vector sizes/windows and whether trained per-fold, (b) similarity threshold sweep (e.g., 0.6, 0.7, 0.8), (c) top-k expansion sizes (5,10,20), (d) PCA dims (50,200,400,800) with associated variance explained, and (e) SVM gamma/C grid results for representative features.

concerns.title: Possible company-level leakage across CV folds
concerns.description: Multiple reports per company (2012–2015 subset has 3892 reports from 1323 companies) could place different reports of the same company in both train and test folds, enabling the model to exploit company-specific patterns and inflate performance.
evidence: 6.1: dataset size and company count provided; 6.2: 5-fold CV used but no mention of grouping by company.
Shared analysis flagged potential company-level leakage (A10).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Re-run CV grouping such that all reports of a given company are confined to a single fold (company-grouped CV). Compare grouped-CV metrics to current CV and report differences.

concerns.title: Stacking procedure sensitivity and limited meta-training data
concerns.description: Stacking uses a 70/30 split of training data to train base and meta models; this reduces effective training data and may be sensitive to the split or to the meta-learner (SVM-RBF). No alternative stacking (k-fold stacking/out-of-fold predictions) or split sensitivity analysis is reported.
evidence: Section 4.3 describes 70/30 stacking and notes potential training data shortage; Table 1 shows stacking best among tested fusion methods but no stability analysis.
Shared analysis suggests stacking may be brittle without ablation.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Implement out-of-fold stacking (k-fold blending) to use all training data for base model fitting and meta-training; test meta-learner variants (linear regressor, tree-based) and report performance variance across different splits.

concerns.title: Outlier filtering of volatility labels may bias evaluation
concerns.description: Filtering volatility labels beyond mean ±3σ removes extremes that might be economically important and changes label distribution; impact on r2/MSE not quantified.
evidence: Section 5: explicit statement of filtering volatility values outside mean ±3σ.
Shared analysis notes potential bias in tail performance.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report experiments with and without outlier filtering (or with alternative robust regression losses), quantify how many samples removed and show effect on metrics and on sector/year distributions.

comparable_works.relevance: Closest prior work using Word2Vec to expand financial lexicons for 10-K sentiment features; serves as a primary baseline and a methodological precedent for lexicon expansion.

If company-grouped CV yields similar gains, then improvements are not due to company-specific leakage and likely generalize across firms.
If stacking gains persist under out-of-fold stacking and alternative meta-models, then fusion claim is robust and computationally practical.

consensus_findings: The proposed embedding-augmented IR weighting (notably the extended BM25 denoted B̂M25) yields higher reported r2 for text-only volatility prediction under the paper's stated pipeline and 2012–2015 subset.

Combining textual features with market features via stacking (as implemented) produced higher reported r2 and lower MSE than text-only, market-only, early fusion, and the MKL configuration reported in the manuscript.

The authors detect year-to-year changes in Risk Factors language and report better predictive performance when restricting to the recent 2012–2015 subset, motivating the paper's decision to focus main experiments on that window.

Per-sector language differences exist and are interpretable at the term level; with the current per-sector sample sizes and modelling choices, sector-specific models did not outperform a pooled general model in the reported experiments.

Key methodological and reporting omissions (Word2Vec training on the full corpus, lack of Risk Factors extraction validation, absence of company-grouped CV, missing hyperparameter/sensitivity analyses, and no statistical tests of metric differences) are widespread concerns across reviewers and materially limit confidence in the generality of the empirical claims.
disagreements: Degree of novelty: some reviewers characterize the contribution as an incremental but useful adaptation of IR embedding-augmentation to financial lexicon weighting; one reviewer frames the transfer as potentially more disruptive for long-form financial text processing. These are differing interpretations, not contradictory facts.

Interpretation of MKL vs stacking results: reviewers agree stacking outperformed MKL in the reported experiments but disagree on whether MKL was fairly tuned/allocated compute; one reviewer highlights possible under-tuning of mklaren as an alternative explanation for MKL's weaker performance.

Weight of evidence for restricting to 2012–2015: reviewers accept that the reported diagnostics (centroid similarity, r2 vs years included) motivate a subset choice, but differ in whether that constitutes sufficient evidence of harmful concept drift versus a dataset/regime selection that may reduce generality.
uncertainty_hotspots: Temporal leakage risk: Word2Vec and LexExt are described as trained on 'the corpus of all reports' — if embeddings saw test-period documents, similarity-based augmentations could leak future linguistic patterns into features and inflate reported gains.

Risk Factors extraction reliability: extraction used heuristic term-matching but no extraction precision/recall or annotated validation is reported; mis-extraction could produce noisy or biased textual inputs.

Cross-validation leakage at company level: the dataset contains multiple reports per company over years; the CV protocol does not clearly state whether folds were grouped by company, so company-specific leakage is plausible.

Hyperparameter and pipeline sensitivity: key choices (similarity threshold = 0.70, top-20 expansion, PCA dim = 400, fixed SVM RBF settings, stacking 70/30 protocol, mklaren/MKL params) are presented without ablation or selection details — method rankings may depend on these settings.

Statistical robustness: reported r2 and MSE are point estimates without fold-level variances, confidence intervals, or paired statistical tests; observed differences may not be statistically significant.
Label handling: outlier filtering of volatility labels (mean ± 3σ) may remove economically important tail events and alter metric interpretation, particularly for risk-focused applications.
model_diversity_effects: Role-oriented emphases produced complementary concerns: structure/logic reviewers prioritized reasoning chains and conditional validity (highlighting dependencies like embedding training and extraction), methodology auditors emphasized reproducibility protocols (per-fold embedding training, grouped CV, hyperparameter reporting), and novelty assessors varied in framing (incremental vs promising) which influenced how they weighed missing controls against the reported gains.

This diversity of reviewer roles led to a richer identification of possible artifact sources (e.g., leakage, extraction noise, tuning effects) than any single role would likely surface alone — increasing the set of critical follow-up experiments necessary to validate claims.

Because reviewers with reproducibility roles repeatedly flagged the same operational risks, the probability mass of plausible alternative explanations for the reported improvements shifted toward methodological artifacts (not necessarily invalidating the idea, but requiring targeted tests).
meta_review.editor_guidance: As central decision-maker, request focused reproducibility and robustness materials and experiments before treating reported performance gains as generalizable: (1) require explicit statements and experiments eliminating temporal leakage — retrain Word2Vec and reconstruct LexExt inside proper training-only data partitions (either per-fold or temporal holdouts) and report how results change; (2) require an annotated validation set for Risk Factors extraction (precision/recall/F1 and qualitative failure modes) and rerun principal experiments on corrected/validated extractions; (3) require grouped cross-validation by company (all reports of a company in one fold) and temporal holdout experiments (train on pre-201X, test on later years) to quantify leakage and generalization; (4) demand per-fold metrics, standard deviations, and formal paired statistical tests (or bootstrap CIs) for the key comparisons (B̂M25 vs best baseline; stacking vs MKL/early fusion); (5) request ablation/sensitivity analyses for similarity threshold, top-k expansion size, PCA dimensions, SVM gamma/C/epsilon, and stacking protocol (out-of-fold stacking) to show robustness; (6) ask for detailed mklaren/MKL hyperparameters or an alternative well-tuned MKL baseline for a fair fusion comparison; (7) require reporting of how many volatility labels were removed by the mean ±3σ filter and results without this filtering (or using robust losses) to assess impact on tail-event performance; and (8) require release of code, seeds, exact fold splits, Word2Vec training scripts, and the Risk Factors extraction code plus the annotated extraction validation set to enable independent replication. Frame these as targeted rebuttal experiments and transparency deliverables rather than open-ended requests.

Cross-validation details: whether folds are grouped by company (company-wise CV) or randomized at the report level; exact train/test file lists and random seeds are not provided.

Hyperparameter search/reporting: PCA selection protocol (what metric and validation splits used), SVM RBF gamma search (or default), C and epsilon search ranges, and mklaren/MKL parameterization are not shown.

epistemic_limits: Current synthesis cannot determine whether the reported empirical improvements reflect a generalizable methodological advance or are partly/wholly explained by methodological artifacts (temporal/company-level leakage, unvalidated extraction, tuning choices). The reviewers' analyses identify concrete experiments that would substantially reduce uncertainty, but absent those re-analyses the evidence base is conditional on the original pipeline's undisclosed choices. Therefore, conclusions about real-world generalizability, economic significance, and method superiority remain provisional. In particular: (a) if retraining embeddings on training-only data preserves the gains, confidence in the method increases markedly; (b) if company-grouped CV and validated Risk Factors extraction significantly reduce reported r2 differences, then the original gains are likely inflated by pipeline artifacts. The synthesis makes no probabilistic claim about which of these outcomes will obtain; resolving that requires the requested reproducibility and robustness experiments and the release of code/data splits. Reviewers' confidence intervals around the core empirical claim reflect this uncertainty and shrink only after the specific validation steps above are completed.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript adapts embedding-augmented IR term-weighting (Eq.3) to lexicon-based sentiment features extracted from 10-K Item 1A (Risk Factors), reduces features via PCA, and uses SVM regression plus fusion with market features (stacking, MKL, early fusion) to predict realized volatility. On a curated 2012–2015 subset (3892 reports) the authors report that embedding-augmented BM25 (B̂M25) improves text-only r2 relative to reproduced lexicon baselines, and that stacking text + market features gives further r2/MSE improvements and greater stability over longer horizons. The paper also documents year-clustering (argued as concept drift) and shows per-sector linguistic differences, concluding that sector-specific models do not outperform a pooled model given current per-sector sample sizes. These findings are supported by multiple experiments, but several methodological and reporting gaps (most importantly possible temporal/company-level leakage, unvalidated Risk Factors extraction, missing hyperparameter/sensitivity studies, and absence of statistical testing) materially limit the degree to which the reported numerical gains can be accepted as generalizable.
strengths: Clear and reproducible-seeming pipeline connecting IR embedding-augmentation (Eq.3) to lexicon-based sentiment features, with the technical idea grounded in prior IR work (Rekabsaz et al.).

Comprehensive empirical comparisons: multiple weighting schemes (standard and augmented), Lex vs LexExt, fusion strategies (early, stacking, MKL), and baselines (Kogan 2009; Wang 2013; Tsai & Wang 2014; GARCH).
Thoughtful temporal and sectoral analyses: year-clustering diagnostics motivate restricting to a recent subset, and per-sector coefficient inspections provide interpretable domain insights.
Practical fusion recommendation: in the reported experiments stacking (late fusion) is a computationally inexpensive approach that outperforms the tested MKL and early fusion configurations.
limitations: Potential temporal leakage: Word2Vec embeddings and LexExt are described as trained on 'the corpus of all the reports' (all years). If embeddings see test-period documents, similarity-based augmentation (R(t), Eq.3) can introduce future-test information into training features and inflate reported performance. The paper does not report experiments retraining embeddings inside training-only partitions.

Risk Factors extraction not validated: Item 1A extraction is done via term-matching heuristics but no annotated validation (precision/recall/F1) or extraction failure analysis is provided. Mis-extraction or inconsistent boundaries could add noise or systematic bias to all text features.

Cross-validation leakage risk at company level: the dataset contains multiple reports per company (1323 companies, 3892 reports) but the CV protocol does not specify whether folds are grouped by company. If reports from the same firm appear in both train and test folds, firm-specific signals could inflate performance.

Insufficient reporting of hyperparameter searches and sensitivity: key choices (Word2Vec hyperparameters and whether embeddings were trained per-fold, similarity threshold = 0.70, top-k expansion, PCA dimension = 400, SVM RBF gamma/C/epsilon, stacking 70/30 protocol, mklaren/MKL parameters) lack ablation or justification; rankings of methods may depend on these settings.

No statistical uncertainty quantification: tables show mean r2 and MSE but not fold-level variances, confidence intervals, or paired statistical tests to establish whether reported improvements are significant and robust.

Label filtering of extreme volatility values (mean ± 3σ) is applied without quantifying how many observations were removed or how their exclusion affects practical/risk-focused performance, especially tail-event prediction.
open_questions: Were Word2Vec embeddings and LexExt constructed using the entire corpus including test-year documents, or were embeddings retrained within training-only partitions (per-fold or temporally)? Please provide experiments that retrain embeddings only on training data and report the effect on the main text-only and Text+Market results.

How accurate is the heuristic Risk Factors (Item 1A) extraction? Please provide an annotated validation set (even modest size, e.g., 100–200 documents) with precision/recall/F1 for extraction and examples of common failure modes; rerun main experiments on the validated/cleaned subset or report sensitivity.

Does cross-validation group reports by company (so all reports for a firm are in the same fold)? If not, please rerun key experiments with company-grouped CV and temporal holdouts (train on earlier years, test on later years) and report differences in r2/MSE and variance.

Provide fold-level results (per-fold r2/MSE), standard deviations, and paired statistical tests (or bootstrap CIs) comparing (a) B̂M25 vs best reproduced baseline and (b) stacking vs MKL/early fusion. Are the reported differences statistically significant?

Please supply ablation/sensitivity analyses for (a) similarity-threshold sweep for embedding-augmentation (e.g., 0.6–0.9), (b) top-k lexicon expansion sizes (e.g., 5/10/20), (c) PCA dimensions (e.g., 50/200/400/800) with variance-explained, (d) SVM hyperparameter grid including RBF gamma, and (e) stacking protocols (out-of-fold stacking vs the reported 70/30 split, alternate meta-learners). How robust are the relative rankings to these choices?

How many volatility labels were removed by the mean ±3σ filter, in which years/sectors do they cluster, and how do results change if filtering is removed or replaced by robust loss functions or explicit tail metrics?
consensus_snapshot: Across reviewers there is agreement that the embedding-augmented IR idea is plausible and that the paper presents consistent point-estimate improvements (B̂M25 and stacking Text+Market) on the reported 2012–2015 subset under the stated pipeline.

All reviewers identify major methodological/reporting omissions (Word2Vec training on full corpus, unvalidated risk-factor extraction, possible company-level leakage, limited hyperparameter/sensitivity reporting, no statistical tests) that need to be addressed to establish generalizability.
Reviewers concur that sectoral language differences exist and are interpretable, but that sector-specific modeling conclusions are conditional on sample sizes and the modelling choices tested.
disagreement_snapshot: Degree of novelty: some reviewers frame the work as an incremental but useful method-transfer from IR to financial sentiment (embedding-augmentation applied to lexicons), while others view the domain application to long-form regulatory filings as a more novel or promising transfer — these are interpretive differences rather than disagreements about empirical facts.

Fairness of MKL comparison: reviewers agree stacking outperformed the MKL configuration reported, but disagree whether mklaren/MKL was sufficiently tuned or whether computational approximations caused MKL to underperform; this affects how strongly to generalize the fusion recommendation.

Interpretation of the decision to restrict to 2012–2015: reviewers accept the diagnostic evidence for year-clustering but differ on whether this justifies restricting experiments (may reduce generality) versus motivating alternative drift-mitigation strategies.
uncertainty_snapshot: Highest-impact uncertainties relate to temporal leakage (embeddings seeing test data) and company-level CV leakage — either could materially reduce the magnitude of reported r2 gains if present.

Secondary uncertainties concern extraction quality of Risk Factors and choice/tuning of PCA/SVM/hyperparameters and stacking protocol — these determine robustness and reproducibility of the reported method ranking.
Absence of statistical testing means we cannot evaluate whether observed differences are robust across folds or could be due to sampling variability.

transparency_notes: The manuscript omits key implementation and validation details necessary for independent replication and for assessing the risk of methodological artifacts: exact Word2Vec training hyperparameters (model variant, vector size, window, min-count, epochs, negative sampling) and whether embeddings were trained per-fold or globally; precise Risk Factors extraction heuristics and an annotated extraction validation set (precision/recall/F1); full cross-validation partitioning policy (report-level vs company-grouped CV) and random seeds; hyperparameter search ranges and selection protocol for PCA dims and SVM (including RBF gamma); mklaren/MKL parameters; counts and temporal/sector distribution of volatility labels removed by the mean ±3σ filter; and per-fold metrics with confidence intervals and paired statistical tests. Release of code, exact fold splits, and the small annotated extraction validation set are necessary transparency items.
